title: Hospitals and First Aid
subtitle: Hospital notices, a broken arm, a first aid course and a paramedic

parts.title: Notices and messages
parts.instructions: For each notice, choose what it means.
notices: VISITING HOURS: Visitors are welcome between 2 p.m. and 8 p.m. only. No more than two people at a bedside at the same time, please.
EMERGENCY ENTRANCE: Use the side door for accidents only. For ordinary appointments, please go to the main reception on the ground floor.
PHARMACY: Show the paper from your doctor at the window. Medicine is ready thirty minutes after you hand it in, and the queue is shorter before noon.
FIRST AID COURSE: Learn how to help someone who is hurt. Saturday 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. in Room 5. Lunch is not provided, so bring your own food.
HAND WASHING: Please clean your hands with the gel before you enter and after you leave every ward. This protects patients and staff.

parts.title: A night in hospital
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last winter, I broke my arm while skating on a frozen lake. At first, I thought it was only a bad bruise, but when my friend Pia tried to lift my hand, I almost shouted with pain. She called an ambulance, and a few minutes later, two paramedics arrived. They were kind and calm, and one of them made a joke that made me laugh.

At the hospital, I had to wait for three hours in a crowded room. A boy with a cut on his head was crying, and an old man next to me was coughing loudly. Finally, a nurse called my name and took me to have an X-ray.

The doctor showed me the picture and said that the bone had broken in two places. I would need a plaster for six weeks. I was disappointed, because I had planned to go skiing in February. 'There will be other winters,' said the doctor, smiling.

I went home at midnight with a blue plaster, and my classmates drew funny pictures on it the next day. Now it is off, and my arm is as good as new. I have promised myself, though, that I will never skate on a lake again without checking how thick the ice is.

questions.prompt: What did the writer first think about the injury?
options: That it would heal by itself
That a friend had hit it
That it was only a bruise
That it was a very serious break
questions.explanation: He thought it was only a bad bruise.

questions.prompt: What did one of the paramedics do?
options: He gave the writer a pain killer
He made a joke to cheer the writer up
He told the writer to stand up
He put a plaster on it
questions.explanation: One made a joke that made him laugh.

questions.prompt: What was unpleasant about the waiting room?
options: It was cold and had no chairs at all
It was far from the X-ray department
It was clean and quiet but very hot
It was crowded and noisy for three hours
questions.explanation: He waited three hours in a crowded room.

questions.prompt: Why was the writer disappointed?
options: He could not go skiing in February
He had to miss his exams at school
He had to stay in hospital for weeks
He missed a party with Pia
questions.explanation: He had planned to go skiing in February.

questions.prompt: What has the writer decided?
options: To stop skating for the rest of his life
To take a first aid course next winter
To check the ice before skating
To buy a better pair of skates
questions.explanation: He will check how thick the ice is.

parts.title: Learning first aid
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Last month, I joined a first aid course at the local hospital. I had never done anything like it before, but my mother thought it was a useful skill to learn. [1] We were divided into groups of six, and each group had a different teacher.

Our teacher was a nurse called Mrs Dale, who had worked in hospitals for twenty years. [2] She showed us how to stop bleeding from a cut and how to put a bandage on a hurt knee.

The most difficult part was learning what to do when someone stops breathing. [3] We practised on a plastic model, pressing on its chest again and again until our arms were tired.

At the end of the day, we took a short test. [4] I was very proud of myself when I received my certificate. [5] Now, whenever I see an accident in a film, I know exactly what I would do.
sentences: About thirty people had come, from teenagers to grandparents.
She had a loud voice and a great sense of humour.
Most of the pupils were hoping to become doctors.
The course was held in a large room on the second floor.
Luckily, I answered nearly all the questions correctly.
It is important to stay calm and call for an ambulance first.
It is a day that I will remember for a very long time.
Some of them had come with their friends from work.

gaps.explanation: About thirty people explains why they were divided into groups.
The teacher is described, and then she showed them first aid actions.
Calling an ambulance is the key step when someone stops breathing, and then they practised.
Answering the questions is about the test, and then he is proud of the certificate.
A day to remember closes the text, followed by the film comment.

It is also important to take some exercise, [2] walking to school or playing a sport with friends. Try to sleep for at least eight hours [3] night. If you feel ill, you should go to see a doctor [4] soon as possible. Do not wait until the problem becomes serious. Finally, remember [5] wash your hands often, especially before meals. parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hi, I’ve come to see my grandmother in Ward Five. Her name is Peters.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Of course. Are you on your own?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, my parents are parking the car, and my brother and sister are coming later.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’m afraid we only allow a few people at the bed. It used to be four, with the old rules, but the ward got crowded and noisy. Now it’s two at a time. Just one would be too strict for a family, and the manager agreed with that.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Then my parents can go first, and my brother and sister can wait in the café.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s fine. Visiting hours are until eight o’clock.

question.prompt: How many visitors can see a patient at once?
question.explanation: The old rule of four visitors has changed and one would be too strict; the new rule is two at a time.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: How did your appointment go, Julia?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Not bad. I was afraid he would send me to hospital for tests, but it’s only a bad flu.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Did he give you any tablets?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: He said I could take something for the pain if I wanted, two tablets after dinner, but he didn’t say I must. The main thing is to stay in bed for three days and drink lots of water.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That sounds easy.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Easy for you! I’m bored already, and I haven’t even started. My sister says she will bring me magazines.

question.prompt: What does the doctor tell her to do?
options: Stay in bed and drink water
question.explanation: She does not have to go to hospital and the tablets are optional; the doctor’s main advice is to stay in bed and drink lots of water.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Excuse me, I have a letter for the X-ray department. Is it on the ground floor?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It used to be, but it moved last spring when they built the new entrance. The ground floor has the pharmacy and the café now.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Oh, so it’s near the pharmacy?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: No, that’s the blood test room next to it. Take the lift to the second floor, turn left, and you’ll see big blue doors.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Thank you. And is there a toilet up there?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Yes, just opposite the lift. Please don’t use the stairs if you have a heavy bag, because they are steep.

question.explanation: It moved from the ground floor last spring; the pharmacy has a blood test room next to it, and the X-ray doors are upstairs on the second floor.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Gary, what happened to your hand? It’s huge.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’d like to say it was a bicycle accident, because that sounds brave, but the truth is boring.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Did you walk into a door? Last year you ran into the glass door at the gym.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That was my nose, not my hand. No, I was cutting onions while I was talking on the phone, and the knife slipped. Seven stitches.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Ouch! Did it hurt?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Only when I saw the blood. Then I nearly fainted, and the nurse laughed at me.

question.prompt: How did the man hurt his hand?
question.explanation: He jokes about a bicycle accident and the glass door was last year, but this time he was cutting onions and the knife slipped.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hello, this is Michelle from Lindon Pharmacy, with a message for Mrs Hall. I think I put the wrong advice on your label. It says before breakfast, but that was only for the first week, which you’ve finished. The second week is different. You take just one tablet a day, and the best moment is after your lunch, with a glass of water. Some people prefer the evening, but it works better with food in the middle of the day. So your next one is tomorrow, not tonight. If you aren’t sure, please phone us on the number on the bag. Have a nice day.

question.prompt: When must the woman take the next tablet?
question.explanation: The label said before breakfast but that was for the first week; the pharmacist says that the best moment is after lunch tomorrow, not in the evening.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So, Earl, did you enjoy your visit to the hospital?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Yes! The nurses were so kind. I thought I’d like to be one, because I love helping, but you have to work nights and I hate staying awake.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: What about your dentist, Mr Carter? You said he was funny.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He is funny, but I don’t want to look at teeth all day. No, I want to be like the person who looked at my leg, Dr Silva, and decide which medicine people need. I’d like to do the operations too.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That takes seven years of study.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I know. I’m ready.

question.prompt: What does the boy want to be?
question.explanation: He likes the nurses but hates nights and does not want to look at teeth; he wants to be like Dr Silva, who decides on the medicine.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Suzanne, thanks for coming. I’m much better, but the hospital food is awful.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: When I found you on the kitchen floor I nearly called an ambulance, and you said you were fine.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Well, I wasn’t! Anyway, that’s the past.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Do you want me to take you home today?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: The doctor says tomorrow at the earliest.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Then tonight I’ll make you something from my kitchen. How about soup?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Perfect, with bread, but no fish, please.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’ll cook it after work and come at seven.

question.explanation: The ambulance was nearly called in the past and he cannot go home until tomorrow; she will cook soup and bring it this evening.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Ross, could you come with me on Thursday to the clinic?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Sure, but do you need a lift? I thought you didn’t like driving in the city.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I do have the car, and I know the road, I’ve been there twice. It’s the doctor. He speaks so fast, and he uses long words. Last time I forgot half of what he said.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Are you nervous about the injection?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: No, the injection is easy. I just want somebody to listen as well, and then we can remember it together.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: How are you feeling, Matilda? Are you bored in here?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: A little, in the afternoons. But I have my books, and my daughter comes every day, so I’m not lonely.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: The food must be terrible.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It’s not great, I’ll admit, but I don’t mind. You should see how the nurses treat us. Last night one stayed with me for an hour because I couldn’t sleep.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s kind of her. Most people only think of doctors.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’d be lost without them. I want to thank them somehow, maybe with a card and a big box of chocolates.

question.explanation: Her daughter visits every day and the food does not bother her; she talks warmly about a nurse who stayed an hour and wants to thank them.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Did you pay for parking at the hospital? Four pounds an hour!

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It’s ridiculous. For a visit of two hours you pay eight pounds, and that’s for people who are already worried about someone.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I know. But the space isn’t the problem, I always find a place.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Right, though the walk is long. Ten minutes to the main door, and I have a bad leg.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I never mind walking. It’s the price that makes me angry. They should offer free parking for patients.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Absolutely. I wrote to the hospital about it last month, but nobody answered.

question.prompt: What do Sally and Timothy agree about the hospital car park?
options: It is too far from the entrance
question.explanation: Both complain about the four pounds an hour; only Timothy complains about the long walk, and Sally says she always finds a space.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Opal, I heard that you got an offer from the private clinic. More money, no weekends!

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: True. It’s tempting, honestly, and I’m tired of the early starts.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So you’re going?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I told them no this morning. It isn’t the money or the hours. I’ve worked with the children’s team for eight years. When a child who was very ill comes back, three years later, to say hello, I can’t leave that.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I understand. I’d stay too, even for a smaller salary. Will you tell your manager today?

question.prompt: Why does Opal refuse the new job?
options: She is happy with her team
question.explanation: The new job offers more money and no weekends, but she says it is not about that; she has worked eight years with the children’s team and does not want to leave.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: You look tired, Alma.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Marco had a temperature at three in the morning. Thirty-eight, nearly thirty-nine. I thought about calling the doctor, but after some medicine it went down and he slept.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So he can go to school tomorrow?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: He says he’s fine and wants to see his friends, but I’m not sure that’s sensible. He’d be tired, and in a class of thirty he could pass it to others. I’ll keep him with me one more day.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Probably wise. Do you want me to look after him this afternoon? I finish early on Fridays.

question.prompt: What does Alma decide about her son tomorrow?
question.explanation: She thought about the doctor but the temperature went down, and he wants school; she says she will keep him with her one more day.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So, how was your first day as a hospital volunteer, Romy?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Honestly, I thought I’d be scared. I was afraid of seeing people in pain.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: And were you?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: A bit at the start, but everyone was so friendly. And the jobs were simple, like pushing books around on a trolley and chatting to patients. One old man told me stories for an hour.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Boring?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Not at all! I enjoyed it much more than I expected. I’m going back on Friday, and I may even do a whole day.

question.prompt: How does Romy feel about her first day as a volunteer?
question.explanation: She was afraid at first but people were friendly, the jobs were simple but not boring, and she enjoyed it more than she expected.

parts.title: A talk about the hospital
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: donna
turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the volunteer team at St Mary’s Hospital. I’m Donna, one of the nurses, and I’ll explain your first day. Please come to the reception desk by nine o’clock. Some of you were told ten, but that was the time of last year’s course, so please be there at nine, because we start with a short talk. Next, what to wear. We give you a shirt. The nurses wear blue and the doctors wear white, so you will have a green one, and people will know that you’re a volunteer. Keep it clean, and wear comfortable shoes. Now, where you will work. Most new volunteers start with the young patients. I always thought that ward was on the second floor, as it was before, but it moved in the summer, and now it is on the third floor. Take the lift on the left. What will you do there? On Wednesdays you bring the library trolley and give out books. The children love them. Some of you asked if you could bring flowers, but we don’t allow them on the ward because of allergies. Breaks are important. You get a free lunch, but please don’t go to the café, because that’s for visitors and it gets crowded. The staff canteen is on the ground floor behind reception, and the food is cheap and surprisingly good. Finally, your promise. We don’t ask for much. After a trial of three months, we hope that you’ll stay for at least six months, because the children get used to you, and it’s sad when a friendly face disappears. One more thing: if you have a cold, please stay at home and phone us, because many of our patients are very weak and they catch things easily. That’s all from me. Does anybody have any questions before we go upstairs?

gaps.explanation: Some were told ten, but that was last year’s course; they must be at reception by nine.

gaps.prompt: Volunteers are easy to recognise by their ___ shirts
gaps.explanation: Nurses wear blue and doctors wear white, so the volunteers have a green one.

gaps.prompt: The young patients are looked after on the ___ floor
gaps.explanation: The ward used to be on the second floor, but it moved in the summer and now it is on the third floor.

gaps.prompt: On Wednesdays, volunteers hand out ___ from a trolley
gaps.explanation: They bring the library trolley and give out books; flowers are not allowed.

gaps.prompt: Volunteers eat their free lunch in the ___
gaps.explanation: The café is for visitors; the staff canteen is behind reception.

gaps.prompt: Volunteers are asked to stay for a minimum of ___ months
gaps.explanation: After a trial of three months, they hope that the volunteers will stay for at least six months.

parts.title: A paramedic
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Jenna, what is a normal day like for a paramedic?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: People expect me to say that I start at five in the morning, and my shift does start early, but that isn’t the interesting part. And it’s never quiet and easy, although some mornings are calm until the radio starts. The truth is that there is no normal day. Yesterday I helped a child with a broken arm, then an old man who fell in his garden, and then a woman who was having a baby in a taxi.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: How long did you train?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: First I studied for three years at university, health and emergency care. I looked at the hospital route as well, which takes six years, but it wasn’t for me. After university came six months in the ambulance with an experienced partner, just watching and learning. A year at a special school was the old way, and it doesn’t exist any more.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What do you find hardest about the job?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Not the driving. We have training for fast driving, and I quite enjoy it. The reports are boring, but you write them in the morning with a coffee. The hardest thing is keeping calm when everybody around me is frightened. The family shouts and cries, and I have to speak slowly and quietly, as if I’m not worried. Inside, I may be very worried.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: When do you feel sad?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Working at night is tiring, but I don’t feel sad then, and a colleague who is late is just annoying. It’s when a patient cannot be saved. We try everything, and sometimes it isn’t enough. I still think about some of those people, even after years.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: How do you relax after a bad day?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: I like films with friends, but I’m usually too tired to go to the cinema. And I read, but I can’t concentrate in the garden because of my neighbour’s radio. The best thing is to take my dog to the beach, whatever the weather. The wind and the water clear my head.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Would you recommend the job?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Not for everyone. It’s tiring, I won’t lie, and driving is not a reason to do it. But if you like people, if you enjoy talking to strangers on the worst day of their life and helping them, then yes, absolutely. It’s the best job I can imagine. Every shift I go home knowing that I did something useful, and not many people can say that. I also work with wonderful colleagues, who are like a second family.

questions.prompt: What does Jenna say about her normal day?
options: It is mostly quiet and easy
questions.explanation: Her shift starts early but that is not the point, and it is not quiet; she says that there is no normal day.

questions.prompt: How long did her training take?
options: Six years on a hospital ward
One year at a special school
Three years at university, then six months
questions.explanation: The hospital route takes six years and the special school is the old way; she did three years at university and six months in the ambulance.

questions.prompt: What does she find hardest?
options: Staying calm when others are frightened
questions.explanation: She enjoys the driving and writes reports with coffee; the hardest thing is keeping calm when everybody around her is frightened.

questions.prompt: When does she feel sad?
options: When a patient cannot be saved
questions.explanation: Night work is tiring and late colleagues are annoying; she feels sad when a patient cannot be saved.

questions.explanation: She is too tired for films, and she cannot read in the garden because of the radio; she takes her dog to the beach.

questions.prompt: Why does she recommend the job?
options: It is good for people who like people
It is a good way to learn driving
It is easy and not tiring
questions.explanation: She says it is tiring and driving is not a reason; she recommends it if you like talking to strangers and helping them.

parts.title: Getting to know you
parts.instructions: Answer each question in your own words. Aim to speak for 20-30 seconds.

questions.prompt: Do you often feel ill? What do you do when you feel ill?
